summary: Bohemian knotweed is the hybrid of Japanese knotweed and giant knotweed. The two parents cross widely, so New York's official ranking form assesses them and their hybrid together, and ranks them Very High. It comes up early, grows fast (up to about 3 inches a day) and forms stands that smother everything beneath them. Its dead stems last through the winter, smothering plants below and creating a fire and flood hazard.
history: Its parent species are native to Asia (China, Japan and Korea). Knotweeds have occasionally been planted for erosion control and sold as garden plants, and they are now found throughout New York State.
seasons: It comes up early in the season and grows quickly; last year's dead stems stay standing through the winter.

handling.text: Pieces of its stems and roots can grow into new plants, and it is extremely difficult to get rid of once established. Seeds and plant fragments can be carried in soil and compost, and pieces can be carried by water.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
